exp_pool.title: Is Watching Porn Cheating in a Relationship?
exp_pool.text: You found porn on your partner’s phone, and now you’re wondering if watching porn is cheating or if you’re overreacting. Or maybe you’re the one whose partner found it, and you genuinely don’t understand why something you never considered cheating suddenly feels like betrayal to them. Either way, you can end up arguing about a question neither of you ever actually said out loud. That’s why couples can so easily talk past each other when it comes to porn. One person is focused on the fact that no touching happened and no one else was in the room. The other is focused on sexual arousal happening outside the relationship and the fact that it was kept from them. When you’ve never talked about what porn means in your relationship, that silence can create a gap between what each of you thought you had agreed to. In this episode of The RISE to Intimacy Podcast, I break down three common myths about porn in relationships, including whether it counts as cheating, whether it harms relationships, and whether regular use means addiction. I also explain what the research actually tells us about when porn creates problems and how to have the conversation that may have needed to happen much earlier. 3:19 - Myth #1: watching porn is either always cheating or never cheating 4:33 - The unspoken assumption almost every couple carries about porn 5:26 - Myth #2: watching porn is bad for relationships across the board 6:40 - The pattern that predicts whether porn will harm your relationship 7:26 - Myth #3: watching porn means you have or are developing an addiction 8:55 - The biggest predictor of whether someone believes they're "addicted" to porn 10:23 - Three things that tie all these myths together (and actually do the relationship damage that porn gets blamed for) 11:54 - Four tips on how you can have a real conversation about porn in your relationship with your partner Mentioned In Is Watching Porn Cheating in a Relationship? It includes upgrades like: Stories that last up to 48 hours Extra Story insights Custom profile tweaks More control over who sees your content Despite the name, Plus isn’t a business tool. smm_pool.title: How to get verified on Instagram in 2026
smm_pool.text: What does Instagram verification mean? Instagram verification is the process of getting a blue checkmark badge that appears next to your username on the platform. The verification badge signals to other users on the platform that an account really belongs to the user, artist, brand, or organization it represents. If you’re looking to enhance your presence while pursuing verification, consider brainstorming unique Instagram username ideas that reflect your brand identity. Your favorite celebrity probably has a blue checkmark on their account: Brands with a strong social media following usually have a verified badge too: But there are actually two types of verification: traditional verification and paid. Originally, verification was only available to “ notable and unique ” people or brands. The process of awarding that coveted blue checkmark was shrouded in mystery, and verification was usually restricted to celebrities and big brand names. These days, users can also pay for verification through Meta Verified . That means anyone can get a verified badge on their Instagram or Facebook accounts. Whichever route you take, the payoff is the same: Legitimacy and trust: The verification process requires a government-issued ID, so having a verified badge establishes your account authenticity and helps the community know it’s the real you. People are more likely to follow, message, and do business with an account they can confirm is genuine. Impersonation protection: Fake accounts exist for all kinds of reasons, from scams to parodies. A badge sets your account apart from impersonators, and Meta Verified adds proactive account monitoring to help protect your account from impersonators or hackers. Visibility and performance: Verified accounts appear at or near the top of comments and search results when people type in a business name. They also appear as a recommended business to follow in the Feed, which can translate into more followers, website clicks, and conversions. Extra features: Verified accounts get access to perks like exclusive stickers on Instagram Stories and Reels to help their content stand out. No matter which method an account used to get verified, the blue checkmark looks the same. That means it’s impossible to know whether it was awarded to a user through traditional means or if they’re paying for the Meta Verified service. smm_pool.title: Buffer Commit: Awarding 10% of a Month’s Profit to up to 16 Apps Built on Our API
smm_pool.text: Today, we finally get to talk about something we've been building behind the scenes for months: Buffer Commit, our first build contest on the Buffer API! We’ll run Buffer Commit every year, and it will grow alongside our builder community. This year, registration is open from October 15, and the build window runs from October 28 to November 13, 2026. Our prize pool is 10% of our net profit for August 2026, which comes to $25,600, shared equally among up to 16 winners for $1,600 or more each. (We lined up the 16 winners and $1,600 as a small nod to Buffer turning 16 on November 30 of this year.) The inspiration for Buffer Commit came alongside our release of Buffer's new public API in May of this year, which we built so that anyone, from a solo creator automating their own posting to a team building a product of their own, could build on top of Buffer. What we've seen in the months since has been incredible, and we're beyond thrilled to be investing in the folks building on our API directly. In this post, I'll share a bit more about the why behind this contest, what Buffer Commit is, who it's for, how it works, and what we hope comes out of year one. Why we're doing this Back in November 2010, Buffer's Founder CEO Joel Gascoigne built the first version of Buffer during a Startup Sprint to solve a problem he was experiencing himself. He wanted a way to space out when his tweets were sent, and it turned out that plenty of other people were looking for the same solution. Buffer has grown a lot since then, but that story still matters to us, because it's a reminder that useful software often starts with one person solving a specific problem in their own work. Sixteen years later, that belief shaped one of the bigger product bets we've made. The API we launched in May is a new product, built over the past year on the same GraphQL foundation that has powered Buffer's own apps since 2019. It was designed from the start to be open to everyone. We launched it without knowing how many people would build on it. We built it for developers, and just as much for the creators, marketers, and small business owners who connect Buffer to the tools they already use. That's why we invested in an MCP server, a CLI, and connector integrations alongside the API itself. Since launch, more than 100,000 users have built with the Buffer API, creating more than 300,000 ideas and 20 million posts through it. smm_pool.title: The Ideal Facebook Cover Photo Size in 2026 (+ 11 Ideas To Make Yours Stand Out)
smm_pool.text: Your cover photo is the biggest image on your Facebook Page , and it's usually the first thing people see when they land there. It's also super easy to get wrong. A design can look great on your laptop, and then you open the Facebook app on your phone, and the edges of your headline are gone (or your profile picture is sitting right on top of an important detail). That happens because Facebook shows the same cover photo in a different frame on desktop and mobile. So it's worth spending a few minutes on the dimensions before you upload, rather than a lot of time repositioning after. If you want to jump right to changing your picture: The recommended Facebook cover photo size is 851 × 315 pixels, according to Meta's Help Center . Upload it as an sRGB JPG under 100 KB, and keep text and logos near the middle so nothing important gets cropped on mobile or desktop. Below, I'll walk through how cropping works on each screen, how to design a cover that fits the rest of your Facebook marketing , and 11 brand examples to borrow ideas from. Key takeaways Upload your Facebook cover photo as an sRGB JPG under 100 KB, or as a PNG if it includes a logo or text. Meta says PNG files can give you a better result. Facebook won't accept a cover photo smaller than 400 × 150 pixels. Facebook fits your cover photo to a 16:9 frame on computers and a 2.4:1 frame on mobile, aligned to the left, so the same image shows differently on each screen. Keep text and logos in the middle of your Facebook cover photo. Your profile picture covers part of the left side, and Facebook may crop the edges to fit different screens. Facebook group covers use 1640 × 856 pixels, and event covers use 1920 × 1005 pixels. The strongest Facebook cover photos do one clear job, like explaining what you do, promoting an event, or announcing a launch. The 11 brand examples below show how.
